Next, sort the monthly series by security and month, and create eleven monthly lags of the monthly illiquidity value. These lags represent the prior eleven months, alongside the current month.

Then, count how many of the twelve values (current plus eleven lags) are non-missing for each security-month. Compute the twelve-month mean only when all twelve values are present; otherwise set the result to missing.

task2.agent_logic: The definition of operating profitability follows Ball, Gerakos, Linnainmaa and Nikolaev (2015). We compute our accruals measure using balance sheet items on Compustat (e.g., changes in accounts receivable, accounts payable, deferred revenue, and inventory). We use the balance sheet to create the cash-based operating profitability and accruals measures, because cash flow statement accruals are available only starting in 1988. Hribar and Collins (2002) show that balance sheet accruals can be affected by large corporate investment and financing decisions such as equity offerings and mergers and acquisitions. In what follows, we therefore also construct the accruals and cash-based operating profitability measures using information from cash flow statements for the post-1988 sample. We provide detailed descriptions and formulas for operating profitability, cash-based operating profitability, and accruals in the Appendix. All profitability measures are deflated by the book value of total assets in year t-1. We then use the Davis, Fama and French (2000) book values of equity from Ken French's website to fill in missing values. Panel A of Table 2 reports the Fama and MacBeth (1973) regressions for the All-but-microcaps sample. When operating profitability and accruals are used in separate regressions, their t-values are 5.29 (column 2) and -6.30 (column 3). When these variables are in the same regression, their t-values increase in absolute magnitude to 5.85 and -8.26 (column 4) and the absolute values of the slope coefficients on operating profitability and accruals are similar in magnitude (2.30 and 2.49). The cash-based profitability measure, however, continues to dominate with a t-value of 9.62 (column 5). Similar to Panel A's sample, cash-based operating profitability continues to dominate in Panel B's sample, which is restricted to microcap stocks. In Panel B, the t-value for operating profitability is 4.76 (column 2), and it decreases to 2.25 (column 4) when operating profitability and accruals are used in the same regression. The t-value for cash-based profitability, however, increases to 10.55 (column 5). The high-minus-low decile portfolio formed on the basis of operating profitability earns a monthly three-factor model alpha of 29 basis points per month with a t-value of 1.84, and for accruals the excess return is -35 basis points per month with a t-value of -2.55. Consistent with the Fama and MacBeth regressions presented in Table 2, the highest excess return is for the cash-based operating profitability strategy—47 basis points per month with a t-value of 3.14. We find similar results when we evaluate the strategies with CAPM and the three-factor model. The high-minus-low decile portfolio formed on the basis of operating profitability earns a CAPM alpha of 42 basis points per month with a t-value of 2.81 and a three-factor model alpha of 74 basis points per month with a t-value of 5.98. The equivalent strategy formed on the basis of accruals earns a CAPM alpha of -43 basis points per month with a t-value of -3.15 and a three-factor model alpha of -39 basis points per month with a t-value of -2.98. Similar to the Fama and MacBeth (1973) regressions presented in Table 2, cash-based operating profitability continues to exhibit the strongest predictive power. The high-minus-low strategy earns a CAPM alpha of 65 basis points per month with a t-value of 4.74 and a three-factor model alpha of 89 basis points per month with a t-value of 8.48. For the profitability strategies, t-values for the high-minus-low decile portfolio are generally larger among small stocks than among big stocks, consistent with the findings of Fama and French (1996). Table 8 presents the tangency portfolio weights along with Sharpe ratios. The (annualized) Sharpe ratio on the market portfolio over the 1963 through 2014 sample period is 0.39, and it increases to 1.06 when we construct the (ex post) mean-variance efficient portfolio using also the size, value, and momentum factors. An investor who trades the market along with these three factors would benefit by adding the accruals factor to the investment opportunity set. By doing so, the Sharpe ratio increases to 1.12. Both operating profitability and cash-based operating profitability are, however, more valuable to the investor than the accruals factor. Adding the operating profitability factor instead of the accruals factor increases the Sharpe ratio to 1.4, and adding the cash-based operating profitability factor increases it to 1.67.
